title: The dhadis
hookLine: ballad-singers with small drums and a fiddle sing the panth's history

lines: THE SONG STOPS; THE STORY STARTS.
cards: Halfway through the song, the singer stops singing and starts talking. A Guru on the move, a martyr who wouldn't bend, a battle at a river: the story comes out plainly, and the crowd leans in.
Then the drum comes back, a small hourglass drum held up in one hand and struck with the other, with a bowed fiddle crying along beside it, and the story turns into song again.
The singers stand rather than sit, and their voices are built to carry across a crowded courtyard. These ballad-singers are today's word.

teach.b: First, the name. A dhadi is a ballad-singer who plays the dhad, that small hourglass drum, usually with a sarangi, the bowed fiddle, beside it. Second, a name a Guru took for himself.

teach.h: GURU NANAK: I WAS A MINSTREL.
teach.b: In a var in Raag Majh, Guru Nanak calls himself a dhadi. In paraphrase: I was a minstrel with no work, and the Lord put me to work, singing praise day and night.
Not a king, not a judge, not a scholar: a wandering ballad-singer, glad to be hired. A humble trade became a Guru's picture of his own calling. Third, history sung.
Tradition says Guru Hargobind welcomed dhadis to sing vars, ballads of courage, at the Akal Takht, the seat he raised facing the Harmandir. This path met the var back on day five hundred thirty-six.
A var praises those who stood firm, so dhadis turned the panth's story into song: the Gurus, the martyrs, the battles, the families who paid a price.
For anyone without a history book, the dhadi was one, out loud, with a drum. Fourth, the way it's done. Song and speech take turns.
The singers give a verse; one steps out and tells the story plainly; the verse returns, and the crowd now knows why it matters.
Dhadi jathas still sing at gurdwaras and gatherings, especially on days that remember martyrs.

how: Dhadi jathas sing vars and ballads of Sikh history with the dhad and sarangi at gurdwaras and gatherings, mixing sung verse with spoken narration, especially on days that remember martyrs.

a ballad-singer with a small hourglass drum
a storyteller who recites without any music

games.q: inside the dhadis: tap the pairs.
p: a ballad praising those who stood firm

s: Guru Nanak called himself a dhadi
in a var in Raag Majh: a minstrel with no work, put to work singing praise.
the dhad is a large drum set on the ground
it's a small hourglass drum, held in one hand and struck with the other.
dhadis only sing and never speak
song and speech take turns: a verse, then the story told plainly, then the verse again.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, looking for a picture of your own calling. which do you choose?
o: a minstrel, a dhadi, put to work.
games.why: in Raag Majh, Guru Nanak calls himself a dhadi: a minstrel with no work, whom the Lord put to work singing praise.

practice: If you can, play a few minutes of a dhadi jatha: the drum, the fiddle, the voices, the spoken story between.
If not, recall one story from your own family told so often it almost sounds like a song, and hear again who first told it.
